title: Largest Permutation
directAnswer: You have a permutation of 1..n and at most k swaps; produce the lexicographically largest result. Greedily walk positions left to right: position i should hold the value n − i (the largest value not yet locked). If it already does, move on; otherwise swap in that value from wherever it currently sits, using a value→index map for O(1) lookup, and spend one swap. Stop when k runs out. O(n) time and space.

remember.pattern: Greedy left-to-right placement of the largest remaining value, with a value→index map for O(1) swaps
remember.formula:
pos[v] = index of value v   # build once
for i in 0..n-1:
    if k == 0: break
    want = n - i              # largest value that belongs at position i
    if arr[i] != want:
        j = pos[want]
        swap arr[i], arr[j]
        pos[arr[j]] = j; pos[want] = i   # update the map for both moved values
        k -= 1
return arr
rules: The input is a permutation of 1..n, so the largest possible value for position i is exactly `n − i` (0-indexed positions).
Greedy is correct: fixing the most significant position with the biggest available value beats any other use of a swap.
Use a value→index map so you can find where the desired value lives in O(1), then swap it into place.
Each productive placement costs exactly one swap; skip positions already holding the right value (they cost nothing).
Stop as soon as `k` hits 0 — remaining positions stay as they are.
whenToUse: Maximise (or minimise) a sequence lexicographically under a bounded number of swaps
Values are a permutation so the target at each position is known in advance
A swap budget caps how many positions you can fix
antiSignals: Only adjacent swaps allowed → bubble-style / inversion counting, not direct placement
Values aren't a permutation → the target at each position isn't simply n − i
You must minimise total swap DISTANCE rather than count → different cost model
Unlimited swaps → just sort, no greedy budget reasoning needed
remember.takeaway: Lexicographic maximisation under a swap budget is a most-significant-digit-first greedy: place the largest legal value at the leftmost position, each fix costing one swap, and keep a value→index map so locating the swap partner is O(1). The exchange argument proves fixing earlier positions first is optimal.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you see that the largest permutation fills positions left to right with n, n−1, n−2, …, and whether you keep a value→index map so each swap is O(1) rather than scanning.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Linear-scanning for the desired value each step (making it O(n·k) or worse), or forgetting to update the map after a swap so later lookups point to stale indices.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Justify greedy with an exchange argument: a swap that raises an earlier position outranks any number of swaps improving later positions, because earlier positions are more significant.

problemStatement:
You are given a permutation of the integers `1` to `n` and a number `k`. You may perform **at most `k` swaps** of any two elements.

Return the **lexicographically largest** permutation obtainable with at most `k` swaps.
constraints: 1 ≤ k ≤ 10⁹  (effectively capped at n − 1 useful swaps)
The input is a permutation of 1..n (each value 1..n appears exactly once)
understanding: Lexicographically largest means the first position should be as large as possible, then the second, and so on. Since the values are exactly 1..n, the ideal sequence is n, n−1, n−2, …. Each position we fix to its ideal value costs one swap (unless it's already correct). With only k swaps, we fix the k most significant out-of-place positions, left to right.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are swaps limited to adjacent elements?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — any two positions can be swapped. That's why one swap can place the global maximum directly at position 0.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the input guaranteed to be a permutation of 1..n?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. That's what makes the target at position i exactly n − i (0-indexed), with no duplicates or gaps.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do we use exactly k swaps or at most k?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: At most k. If the array is already largest, or becomes largest before k runs out, we stop early — wasting a swap can only hurt.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What if k exceeds n?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: At most n − 1 swaps are ever useful (the last position auto-fixes once the rest are correct). Extra budget is simply unused.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Search All Reachable Permutations
approaches.whenToMention: Mention to frame the search space, then collapse with the greedy observation.
hints: With at most k swaps, the reachable set is every permutation within k swaps of the start. You could BFS/DFS that space and keep the largest.
Each state branches into C(n,2) ≈ n²/2 possible swaps; depth up to k. The tree has on the order of (n²)^k leaves.
Even n = 100 and k = 5 is astronomically large. It only confirms what greedy gives directly.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each of up to k swap levels branches over ~n²/2 swaps; the reachable-permutation tree is roughly (n²/2)^k states. Exponential in k.
approaches.explanation:
Define the search space as all permutations reachable with at most `k` swaps from the input. Explore it (DFS/BFS), comparing each reachable permutation and keeping the lexicographically largest.

**Why it's correct.** Every sequence achievable within the budget is generated, so the maximum among them is the answer.

**Why it's hopeless.** Each step can swap any pair — about `n²/2` choices — and we may take up to `k` steps, giving an exponential `(n²/2)^k` tree. For the given constraints this is impossible.

**The structure it reveals.** Compare any two reachable permutations: whichever has a larger value at the *first differing position* wins, regardless of everything after. So spending a swap to raise an earlier position always beats spending it later. That single fact says: process positions left to right, and at each one place the largest value you can — no search needed.
approaches.insight: Lexicographic comparison is dominated by the earliest differing position, so a swap that improves an earlier index is worth more than any swap improving a later one. Greedy left-to-right placement is therefore optimal — the brute-force tree collapses to a single pass.

approaches.name: Greedy — Place Largest Value Leftmost with a Value→Index Map (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Phrase it as 'put n at the front, then n−1, … each costing one swap, until the budget is gone'.
hints: The largest permutation of 1..n is n, n−1, …, 1. So position i (0-indexed) wants the value n − i.
If position i already holds n − i, it's free — move on. Otherwise you must bring n − i here, which costs one swap.
To swap in O(1), keep a map from value to its current index. After swapping, update the map for BOTH values that moved, then decrement k.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Building the value→index map is O(n); the single left-to-right pass does O(1) work per position (map lookup + swap + two map updates). Total O(n) time, O(n) space for the map.
approaches.explanation:
The lexicographically largest arrangement of `1..n` is the descending sequence `n, n−1, …, 1`. So at position `i` (0-indexed) the ideal value is `n − i`. Walk positions left to right; at each one, if the ideal value isn't already there, swap it in from its current location and spend one swap. Stop when `k` reaches 0.

**Why most-significant-position-first is optimal — the exchange argument.** Lexicographic order is decided at the *first* position where two sequences differ. Suppose an optimal solution does NOT place the largest available value at the leftmost still-improvable position `i`, but instead uses a swap to improve some later position `j > i`. Re-route that one swap to instead place `n − i` at position `i`. The new sequence is larger at position `i` than the optimal was (it now holds the max possible value there), and positions `0..i−1` are unchanged — so it is lexicographically ≥ the supposed optimum, using no more swaps. Hence there's always an optimal solution that fixes the leftmost improvable position first; induction gives the full greedy.

**Why a value→index map.** To place `n − i` we must know *where* it currently sits. A map keyed by value gives that in O(1). The naive alternative — scanning for it — is O(n) per position and O(n·k) overall, which is too slow.

**Why we update the map after each swap.** Swapping `arr[i]` and `arr[j]` moves two values. The value `n − i` now lives at `i`, and the value previously at `i` now lives at `j`. Both map entries must be corrected, or a later lookup will point at a stale index and corrupt the result.

**Why skipping correct positions matters.** If `arr[i]` already equals `n − i`, fixing it would 'cost' a wasted self-swap. We skip it for free, preserving budget for positions that actually need it.
approaches.insight: This is most-significant-digit-first greedy. Because the array is a permutation, the target at each index is known (n − i), so there's no search — just locate-and-swap with an O(1) map. The reusable kernel: 'maximise lexicographically under a move budget' → fix earliest positions first, each move buying the biggest legal improvement.

pitfalls: Linear-scanning for the desired value each step → O(n·k), too slow.
Forgetting to update BOTH map entries after a swap → stale indices corrupt later placements.
Spending a swap when arr[i] already equals n − i → wastes budget (guard with the equality check).

commonMistakes: Scanning for the desired value instead of using a value→index map.
Not updating the map after a swap, so later lookups use stale indices.
Swapping even when the position already holds the correct value, wasting a swap.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Linear scan instead of a value→index map
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Searching the array for n − i every step is O(n) per position → O(n·k) overall, which TLEs for large n.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
for i in range(n):
    want = n - i
    if arr[i] != want:
        j = arr.index(want)   # O(n) scan
        arr[i], arr[j] = arr[j], arr[i]
        k -= 1
        if k == 0: break

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Stale map after swap
commonMistakesDetailed.why: After swapping, both moved values changed index. Updating only one (or neither) makes future lookups point to the wrong slot.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wasting a swap on an already-correct position
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If arr[i] already equals n − i, performing a self-swap decrements k for no gain, possibly leaving a later position unfixed.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
for i in range(n):
    if k == 0: break
    j = pos[n - i]
    arr[i], arr[j] = arr[j], arr[i]   # swaps even when i == j
    k -= 1
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
for i in range(n):
    if k == 0: break
    want = n - i
    if arr[i] != want:
        j = pos[want]
        arr[i], arr[j] = arr[j], arr[i]
        pos[arr[j]] = j; pos[want] = i
        k -= 1
